speaker: hassan
text: Welcome to mission control! I'm Dr. Hassan Nasr, your flight director. Today we design a satellite to watch over the Nile Delta's farms and water.

speaker: hassan
text: These seven meters are your limits. Every choice moves several of them at once — that's real mission design.

speaker: hassan
text: Your Mission Commander picks the orbit, the mission length and the rocket. A sun-synchronous orbit gives the same lighting every day — perfect for comparing crops.

speaker: hassan
text: Each rocket lifts a certain mass to each orbit. Heavier spacecraft need bigger, pricier rockets.

speaker: hassan
text: The Science Lead chooses instruments. Each one adds science — and also mass, power, cost and data.

speaker: hassan
text: Hover over the Thermal Infrared Imager. See the meters preview the change before you even click?

speaker: hassan
text: The Spacecraft Engineer feeds the instruments: solar arrays for power, a battery for the shadow, propellant for keeping the orbit.

speaker: hassan
text: If the load is higher than generation, instruments switch off. Keep at least 15% margin — arrays weaken every year.

speaker: hassan
text: Data is worthless until it reaches Earth. The Comms Officer picks the radio and the ground stations.

speaker: hassan
text: Our starter S-band radio cannot keep up with the imager. Try the X-band transmitter and watch this turn green.

speaker: hassan
text: When you're ready, open the readiness review. Red means NO-GO — read why, fix it, then sign off.

speaker: hassan
text: Then launch! Surprises will happen during the mission. Choose wisely — and remember, there's no single perfect design.

speaker: hassan
text: The Nile Delta feeds millions, and water is precious. A satellite that sees crop health can tell farmers where to irrigate.

speaker: hassan
text: We need a multispectral imager or a camera, at least two years in orbit. The budget is modest — spend wisely.

speaker: hassan
text: Dust storms and flash floods can strike in hours. Forecasters need eyes that never blink.

speaker: hassan
text: Carry a sounder or a thermal imager and watch for five years. Which orbit lets you stare at one region all the time?

speaker: hassan
text: Future crews will need water on the Moon — to drink, to breathe, even to make rocket fuel.

speaker: hassan
text: Bring a neutron spectrometer to sniff out hydrogen, plus an altimeter or thermal imager to map the craters. Deep-space comms are a must.

speaker: hassan
text: Two jobs at once: study the Martian air, and relay data for the rovers below.

speaker: hassan
text: Mars is far: weak sunlight, a 12-minute radio delay, and launch windows every 26 months. Miss it and we wait two years.

speaker: hassan
text: We want light that left the first galaxies 13 billion years ago. It arrives as faint infrared heat.

speaker: hassan
text: An infrared telescope must be very cold and very steady. Somewhere far from Earth's warmth would be ideal…

speaker: hassan
text: Sandbox mode: no limits. Build anything and see what happens.

speaker: hassan
text: Try extremes. No battery? A giant radar on a tiny bus? The report will tell you why.

speaker: hassan
